turns.user: im doing weekly meal prep for the first time and i keep reading that you should cook proteins and carbs separately and store them in separate containers. why? like is it food safety or is it just about texture? im an undergrad and cook maybe twice a week so i want to understand the actual reason before i decide if its worth the extra containers
turns.assistant: It's both, but the texture part is what people notice first. Rice, pasta and potatoes keep absorbing moisture from sauces and dressings as they sit, so by day three they're mushy. Proteins like chicken or fish dry out or get rubbery when reheated with starchy food, and they're also more sensitive to time and temperature. Food safety is more about cooking and cooling: you want proteins cooked to a safe internal temperature, then cooled and refrigerated quickly, ideally within two hours. Keeping the components separate lets you control moisture and reheating better. If you only cook twice a week, you can skip most of the extra containers. Just put sauce in a small separate cup and reheat the protein and the starch together.

Step 4: Follow the 10 percent rule loosely, meaning don't increase weekly mileage by more than about 10 percent. turns.user: ok what do i do if i miss a long run, do i just skip it or double up on the next one

If you miss two long runs in a row, drop the next long run back by a mile or two from where you were before, then continue building from there. You're more likely to hit race day healthy if you stay conservative in the middle weeks.

turns.user: i accidentally committed to main instead of my feature branch. how do i move the commit to a new branch without messing up the remote
turns.assistant: Create the branch from where you are now, so it has the commit: git branch my-feature. That leaves your commit on both main and my-feature. Then move main back one commit: git reset --hard HEAD~1, which only changes local main. Because the commit hasn't been pushed, the remote isn't affected. Check git log --oneline on both branches before you do the reset so you know exactly which commit you're removing.

turns.assistant: Yes, you can run the reset now. The changes aren't deleted, because the commit is still on my-feature. The reset only moves the main pointer back one commit. The one thing to watch is uncommitted work: --hard also throws away any uncommitted changes in your working directory, so commit or stash anything else first. If you want a safer version, use git reset --keep HEAD~1 instead, which refuses to run if you have uncommitted changes to files it would touch.

turns.user: ok did it. now i want to pull main to make sure im up to date but git says my branch has diverged
turns.assistant: That usually means local main and origin/main have each moved past their shared commit. Run git fetch first, then compare with git log --oneline main..origin/main and git log --oneline origin/main..main. The first shows commits on the remote that you don't have locally. The second shows commits that are only local. If the second list is empty, your local main is just behind, and git pull --ff-only will fast-forward it. If it has commits you don't recognize, check them before you do anything, because a reset would discard them.
